name.text: WAT 07.1: Negative Is Not an Error!

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write one function, edges, that reports the ends of a list and its length.

How this works in Python

Java gives you two ordered types and neither one counts backwards.

int[] readings = {12, 7, 9, 4, 18};
int first = readings[0];
int last  = readings[readings.length - 1];
int size  = readings.length;

List<Integer> more     = List.of(12, 7, 9);
int           alsoLast = more.get(more.size() - 1);

Python has one type for both jobs. A list is written with square brackets, holds its items in order, and grows and shrinks as you work. It is the counterpart of ArrayList rather than of a Java array, and you never declare its length.

readings = [12, 7, 9, 4, 18]

Three differences to take on board.

  • You read an item with square brackets, the same as a Java array. readings[0] is 12. There is no .get().
  • You ask for the length with len(readings), not readings.length and not readings.size(). len is a function you call on the list rather than something you ask the list for.
  • A negative index counts back from the right. readings[-1] is the last item and readings[-2] is the one before it. Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for a negative index, so this is the reflex to break. Write readings[-1] and never readings[len(readings) - 1].

Running off the end still raises. readings[9] on a five-item list raises IndexError, which is Python's ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Python has no checked exceptions, so nothing in a signature warns you that it can happen.

A list holds anything, and the items need not agree. [12, "kea", 2.5] is a perfectly ordinary list. There is no List<Integer> to satisfy and no boxing to think about.

Your task

Write one function.

  • edges(readings) returns a list holding five values in this order. The first item, the second item, the last item, the second to last item, and how many items there are.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write the body as a single return statement that builds one list.
  • Do not write len(readings) - 1 inside square brackets. A negative index already knows where the end is.
  • Do not write a loop.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

question.answerpreload: def edges(readings): # TODO: return [first, second, last, second to last, how many]
question.answer: def edges(readings): return [readings[0], readings[1], readings[-1], readings[-2], len(readings)]

testcode.text: pair = [3, 1] print(edges(pair)) try: print(pair[9]) except IndexError as problem: print("IndexError:", problem) print(pair[-1], pair[-2])

expected.text: [3, 1, 1, 3, 2] IndexError: list index out of range 1 3

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(edges) assert "for " not in src, "rule broken: no loops" assert "while " not in src, "rule broken: no loops" assert "len(readings) -" not in src, "rule broken: use a negative index, not len() minus one" assert "len(readings)-" not in src, "rule broken: use a negative index, not len() minus one" assert src.count("return") == 1, "rule broken: one return statement" print(edges(["kea", "tui", "moa", "weka"])) print(edges([2.5, 0.0, 9.75]))

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write three functions, channel, newest and trimmed, that cut windows out of a list of samples.

How this works in Python

Java reads part of a list with subList, and subList cannot skip. Taking every second item means writing the counting loop yourself.

List<Integer> window = samples.subList(2, samples.size() - 2);

List<Integer> evens = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < samples.size(); i += 2) {
    evens.add(samples.get(i));
}

Python replaces both with one piece of syntax. A slice is written samples[start:stop:step] inside square brackets. It returns a new list and leaves the original alone.

  • The start is included and the stop is excluded, exactly as subList excludes its end. samples[2:5] takes items 2, 3 and 4.
  • The step is how far Python moves along the list between one item and the next. samples[::2] takes every second item, starting at the front.
  • Leave a number out and Python fills in the end of the list for you. samples[2:] runs from item 2 to the last item, and samples[:5] runs from the front to item 4.
  • A negative bound counts back from the right, so samples[:-2] stops two short of the end.

Here is the shape you are working with. A logger writes two channels into one flat list, taking a sample from each in turn.

flat = [10, 90, 11, 91, 12, 92]
#       c0  c1  c0  c1  c0  c1

Pulling one channel back out is a start and a step together. flat[0::2] is channel zero and flat[1::2] is channel one. Java needs a loop and a counter for the same job.

The trap

samples[-count:] looks like the way to take the last count items, and it is, right up until count is zero. -0 is 0, so samples[-0:] means samples[0:], which is the whole list. Ask for nothing and Python hands back everything. That bug reads as correct in review and only shows up in the data.

Your task

Write three functions. Each one returns a value and none of them prints.

  • channel(samples, index) returns every sample belonging to that channel, where two channels are interleaved, channel zero first.
  • newest(samples, count) returns the last count samples in their original order. A count of zero returns an empty list.
  • trimmed(samples) drops the first two and the last two samples and returns what is left.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Build every result with a slice.
  • Do not call len(). A negative bound already counts from the right.
  • Do not write a loop, and do not call range(), append() or reversed().
  • Guard the zero count and nothing else. A slice that runs off the end returns what it can reach, so a short list needs no help from you.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: odd = [10, 90, 11, 91, 12] print(channel(odd, 0)) print(channel(odd, 1)) print(newest(odd, 3)) print(newest(odd, 1)) print(newest(odd, 0))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (channel, newest, trimmed)) assert "for " not in whole, "rule broken: no loops" assert "while " not in whole, "rule broken: no loops" assert "len(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not call len()" assert "range(" not in whole, "rule broken: no range" assert ".append(" not in whole, "rule broken: no append" assert "reversed(" not in whole, "rule broken: no reversed()" short = [5, 6, 7, 8] print(trimmed(short)) print(trimmed([5, 6, 7])) print(newest(short, 99)) print(channel([], 0), channel([], 1)) print(newest([], 0), newest([], 2))

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write four functions that take a byte frame and a string apart using slices.

How this works in Python

Java gives you a different method for every sequence type. Not one of them can skip items as it goes.

List<Integer> head  = frame.subList(0, 4);
String        start = line.substring(0, 4);
int[]         chunk = Arrays.copyOfRange(bytes, 0, 4);
Collections.reverse(frame);            // changes frame itself

Python replaces all four with one piece of syntax. A slice is written sequence[start:stop:step] inside square brackets. It returns a new sequence and leaves the original alone.

Square brackets also build a list, which is the Python counterpart of ArrayList. The list below holds twelve bytes.

frame = [170, 1, 0, 12, 72, 101, 108, 108, 111, 33, 4, 210]
print(frame[0:4])       # [170, 1, 0, 12]

These eight forms cover the whole feature.

  • frame[0:4] takes items 0, 1, 2 and 3. The stop is excluded, exactly as subList excludes its end.
  • frame[:4] means the same thing. Leave a bound out and Python fills in the end of the sequence for you.
  • frame[4:] runs from item 4 to the last item.
  • frame[-2:] takes the last two items. A negative index counts back from the right, so -1 is the last item and -2 is the one before it.
  • frame[4:-2] starts at item 4 and stops two short of the end.
  • frame[::2] takes every second item. The third number is the step, which is how far Python moves along the sequence between one item and the next.
  • frame[::-1] walks backwards and hands you the whole sequence reversed.
  • frame[:] copies the whole sequence. You get a new list holding the same items.

Java throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when a bound runs off the end. A Python slice cuts the bound back to the end of the sequence instead. Ask a twelve-byte frame for frame[99:200] and an empty list comes back with no error at all. Ask the same frame for frame[99] and Python raises IndexError. One number in square brackets is an index, and an index raises. Two numbers separated by a colon are a slice, and a slice returns whatever it can reach.

That difference hides bugs. A slice that returns nothing looks exactly like a slice that worked, so the tests stay green while the data goes missing. This exercise asks you to call the out-of-range slice yourself and read what comes back.

A string is a sequence too, so every form above works on one. "Kaitaia"[::-1] gives "aiatiaK". Python has no StringBuilder.reverse() because the step already does the job.

Your task

Write four functions. Each one returns a value and none of them prints.

  • carve(frame) returns a list holding five slices of frame in this order. The four-byte header, the payload sitting between the header and the last two bytes, the last two bytes, the whole frame reversed, and every second byte.
  • far_slice(frame) returns frame[99:200]. Run the tests and see what a clamped slice hands back.
  • copy_of(frame) returns a copy of the whole frame.
  • reverse_text(text) returns the string reversed.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write each function body as a single return statement. Assign nothing, so no index variable exists anywhere.
  • Do not call len(). A negative index already knows where the end is.
  • Do not write a loop, and do not call reversed(), list() or range().
  • Do not guard against a short frame. Run the tests and find out what the clamped slice does instead.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: frame = [170, 1, 0, 12, 72, 101, 108, 108, 111, 33, 4, 210] print(far_slice(frame)) try: print(frame[99]) except IndexError as problem: print("IndexError:", problem) print(reverse_text("Kaitaia")) print(reverse_text("radar"))

expected.text: [] IndexError: list index out of range aiatiaK radar

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (carve, far_slice, copy_of, reverse_text)) assert "for " not in whole, "rule broken: no loops" assert "len(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not call len()" assert "reversed(" not in whole, "rule broken: the step reverses, not reversed()" assert "list(" not in whole, "rule broken: no list()" assert ".append(" not in whole, "rule broken: no append" assert "range(" not in whole, "rule broken: no range" assert " = " not in whole, "rule broken: assign nothing, one return statement each" assert whole.count("return") == 4, "rule broken: one return per function" short = [7, 8] print(carve(short)) print(far_slice(short)) twin = copy_of(short) print(twin == short, twin is short) twin.append(9) print(short, twin)

questiontext.text:
Goal

You rewrite three AI-written functions so they read as Python without changing what they return.

How this works in Python

This one is a code review. The three functions below were written by an AI, they are already in the starter box, and every test passes.

Passing tests is not the same as the code being right

Tests check behaviour. They say nothing about whether the next person can read the code, whether an index can drift out of step with the item it is meant to point at, or whether the shape belongs in the language at all. At work you will be reviewing AI-written Python in a safety-critical codebase, where the suite going green is the beginning of the review rather than the end of it. This question is that review, on a small scale.

Here is the Java the AI was thinking in, whether it knew it or not.

for (int i = 0; i < readings.size(); i++) {
    System.out.println(i + ": " + readings.get(i));
}

And here is what it wrote.

def label_readings(readings):
    labels = []
    for i in range(len(readings)):
        labels.append(f"{i}: {readings[i]}")
    return labels


def positions_over(readings, limit):
    hits = []
    for i in range(len(readings)):
        if readings[i] > limit:
            hits.append(i)
    return hits


def total_power(readings):
    total = 0
    for i in range(len(readings)):
        total = total + readings[i]
    return total

One habit, repeated three times. range(len(readings)) builds a run of numbers, and then every line inside the loop pays for it by indexing back into the list. The number is a middleman. Python does not need one.

  • A for loop over a list hands you the items directly. for reading in readings gives you each reading in turn, and there is no index to get wrong.
  • When you genuinely need the position, enumerate hands you both. for i, reading in enumerate(readings) binds i to the position and reading to the item on every pass. It counts from zero, the same as the list does.

Two of the three functions need the position. The third never uses it and should not be asking for it.

Your task

Rewrite all three so they read as Python.

  • label_readings(readings), rewritten.
  • positions_over(readings, limit), rewritten.
  • total_power(readings), rewritten.

The behaviour must not change by a single character of output. The visible tests check that it has not, and a hidden test checks that the range(len(...)) shape is gone, so a rewrite that keeps the old shape fails even though the output is right.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write range(len(...)) anywhere.
  • Use enumerate in the two functions that need a position.
  • The function that needs no position must not ask for one. No enumerate in that one.
  • Keep every return value exactly as it is today. This is a rewrite, not a redesign.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed for discussion. The code below came from an AI and it passes every test. Your job is to judge it, so do not ask an AI whether it is good.

testcode.text: readings = [12, 47, 9, 63, 47] print(positions_over(readings, 40)) print(positions_over(readings, 100)) print(total_power(readings)) print(total_power([])) print(label_readings([]))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (label_readings, positions_over, total_power)) assert "range(len(" not in whole, "rule broken: the range(len(...)) shape is still there" assert "range(len (" not in whole, "rule broken: the range(len(...)) shape is still there" assert "enumerate(" in inspect.getsource(label_readings), "rule broken: number the items with enumerate" assert "enumerate(" in inspect.getsource(positions_over), "rule broken: number the items with enumerate" assert "enumerate(" not in inspect.getsource(total_power), "rule broken: total_power never uses the position, so do not ask for one" print(label_readings(["kea", "tui"])) print(positions_over([2.5, 9.0, 2.5], 3)) print(total_power([1.5, 2.5]))
